Model selection: the evidence for the number of classes

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/model-selection.Rmd
model-selection.Rmd

In finite mixture modelling, the number of latent classes is not known a priori and is not a parameter of the model; it must be determined by comparing models fitted with different numbers of classes. No single statistic identifies the correct number: information criteria, likelihood-based tests and indices of classification quality each have known limitations, and they frequently disagree (Nylund, Asparouhov and Muthén, 2007). Class enumeration is therefore an inferential judgement that integrates several sources of evidence and is reported transparently. This guide describes each source of evidence that latents computes for a set of candidate models: its definition, its interpretation, and the conditions under which it is unreliable. It then outlines how these sources are combined into a defensible and reproducible decision. A complete applied example is given in Class enumeration in mixture models.

The evidence considered here addresses five distinct questions, summarized below together with the functions that report it.

Question Evidence Functions
Which candidate balances fit and size best? Information criteria and their minima as.data.frame(), get_results(x, "best"), plot(x)
Where do added classes stop paying off? Changes between neighbouring candidates and the knee of each curve get_results(x, "deltas"), get_results(x, "knees"), plot(x, what = "deltas"), plot(x, what = "heatmap")
Are the classes distinct? Entropy, average posterior probability, odds of correct classification get_results(x, "classification"), plot(x, what = "diagnostics")
Can the estimate be trusted? Convergence, boundary estimates, replication of the best likelihood, the smallest class plot(x, what = "trust"), plot(x, what = "smallest")
Is one more class supported? The bootstrap likelihood ratio test of neighbouring candidates bootstrap_lrt()

plot(x, what = "selection") displays the evidence of the second, third and fourth rows jointly, and compare_models() tabulates selected candidates side by side.

library(latents)

The candidates

The examples use course_engagement, in which course enrolments are nested within students and each enrolment is described by five standardized indicators of activity. A model is fitted for every combination of one to six profiles and one to four group classes, with class-specific variances and no covariances ("VVI"). Three random starts per candidate are used to limit computation; applied analyses should use at least ten, because replication of the maximum likelihood across starts is itself part of the evidence.

activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
models

The grid comprises 24 candidates, of which 21 were estimated. A model with one profile and several group classes is not identified, because group classes defined over a single profile cannot differ; such candidates are listed but not estimated. Each candidate is labelled by its numbers of classes (e.g., profiles4_groups3 for four profiles and three group classes), and the functions below accept this label.

Before fitting: starts, scaling and missing values

Three analytic decisions precede estimation. Each is passed through the ... argument of enumerate_classes(), enumerate_lpa() and enumerate_lca(), so that it applies identically to every candidate, and each should be reported alongside the selected number of classes.

Random starts

The likelihood of a finite mixture model is typically multimodal, and the EM algorithm converges to a local maximum determined by its starting values. n_starts sets the number of random starts per candidate; increasing it reduces the probability that a candidate is reported at a local rather than the global maximum. A solution at a local maximum usually separates its classes less well, so re-estimation with more starts frequently increases entropy and AvePP. When more starts are required, the entire grid is re-estimated with the same number; re-estimating only the candidates of interest would confer on them an advantage in likelihood and separation that the remaining candidates were not given.

models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 20, seed = 1)

Additional starts also make a degenerate solution more likely to be found when a candidate has more profiles than the data support: one profile collapses on a single observation, with every variance at its lower bound (min_variance). The Gaussian likelihood of such a profile increases without limit as its variances shrink, so its value, and every criterion computed from it, is determined by min_variance rather than by the data, and BIC can favour one profile too many as a result. In a simulation with 500 starts per candidate, this occurred in two of 29 datasets; with ten or twenty starts it was rare. Such candidates carry boundary = TRUE in the table of candidates. boundary = "exclude" sets aside every start with a variance at its lower bound and retains the best of the remaining starts; the default, "allow", retains the highest likelihood, as Mplus does. The option is advisable when many starts are used, and it has no effect on categorical indicators, which have no variances.

models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 200,
                            boundary = "exclude", seed = 1)

Centring and scaling

centering subtracts a mean and scaling divides by a standard deviation, each computed at one of two levels: over all observations ("grand") or within each group ("person"). Combined, they yield the conventional z-scores. Grand-mean standardization (centering = "grand", scaling = "grand") expresses each indicator in sample standard deviations; within-person standardization (centering = "person", scaling = "person") expresses each observation as a deviation from its own group’s mean in units of that group’s standard deviation, so that the profiles describe within-person fluctuation rather than between-person level.

Under covariance structures that estimate a separate variance for each indicator (EEI, VVI, EEE, VVV, EVI, VEI), grand-mean scaling is a reparameterization: it alters the units of the estimates but leaves class membership, entropy and AvePP unchanged. The spherical structures EII and VII constrain all indicators to a common variance, so that an unscaled indicator with a large range would dominate the classification; under these structures the indicators should be standardized beforehand.

srl_indicators <- c("cognitive_strategies", "intrinsic_value",
                    "self_efficacy", "self_regulation", "test_anxiety")
spherical <- enumerate_lpa(srl, srl_indicators, n_profiles = 2:4,
                           model = "EII", centering = "grand",
                           scaling = "grand", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
get_results(spherical, "best")
#>    criterion  convention candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model value
#> 1        aic        <NA> profiles4          4               1   EII  3372
#> 2        kic        <NA> profiles4          4               1   EII  3399
#> 3        bic      groups profiles4          4               1   EII  3461
#> 4        bic individuals profiles4          4               1   EII  3461
#> 5      sabic      groups profiles4          4               1   EII  3385
#> 6      sabic individuals profiles4          4               1   EII  3385

#> 14       clc individuals profiles4          4               1   EII  3433

Because scaling shifts the log likelihood by a constant, information criteria are comparable only among candidates estimated under the same centring and scaling, as is the case within a single grid.

Missing values

With missing = "fiml", the likelihood of each observation is evaluated over its observed indicators, without imputation; under the missing-at-random assumption this yields unbiased estimates. An observation with all indicators missing contributes nothing to the likelihood, and its posterior probability equals the prior implied by its group; it is therefore not classified. Following Mplus, such observations are excluded from the sample size of the individual-level information criteria, from entropy and AvePP, from the classification tables and from the effective class counts; n_informative records the number retained, and the printed fit reports the number excluded. Groups in which no observation has an observed indicator are excluded from the group-level sample size and statistics on the same grounds (n_informative_groups), whereas a group with at least one observed row is retained. Partially observed rows remain in every statistic: they are classified, with correspondingly greater uncertainty, from the indicators available. Setting drop_empty = FALSE restores the counting rules of latents 0.9.37 and earlier, so that previously reported results can be reproduced.

set.seed(3)
incomplete <- course_engagement
empty <- sample(nrow(incomplete), 150)
incomplete[empty, activity] <- NA
partial <- setdiff(sample(nrow(incomplete), 150), empty)
incomplete[partial, "attendance"] <- NA
incomplete_fit <- multilpa(incomplete, activity, "student", n_profiles = 3,
                           n_group_classes = 2, model = "VVI",
                           missing = "fiml", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
get_results(incomplete_fit, "entropy")
#>         level n_classes n_units entropy_sum relative_entropy
#> 1 individuals         3    1272      321.52            0.770
#> 2      groups         2     106        5.42            0.926

Individual-level entropy is computed over 1272 observations: the 1,422 enrolments less the 150 with no observed indicator. Deleting those rows from the data yields identical estimates, likelihood and classification statistics. Deleting partially observed rows, by contrast, alters the sample and, where missingness depends on observed values, biases the estimated profiles.

Information criteria

Definitions

Each criterion adds a penalty to the deviance, -2L, where L is the maximized log likelihood. Let q denote the number of free parameters, n the sample size, and EN = -sum(p log p) the classification entropy, summed over all units and classes of the posterior probabilities p:

Criterion Formula Penalty depends on Reference
aic -2L + 2q parameters only Akaike (1974)
kic -2L + 3(q + 1) parameters only Cavanaugh (1999)
bic -2L + q log(n) sample size Schwarz (1978)
sabic -2L + q log((n + 2) / 24) sample size Sclove (1987)
caic -2L + q (log(n) + 1) sample size Bozdogan (1987)
icl -2L + q log(n) + 2 EN sample size and classification Biernacki, Celeux and Govaert (2000)
awe -2(L - EN) + 2q (1.5 + log(n)) sample size and classification Banfield and Raftery (1993)
clc -2L + 2 EN classification only Biernacki and Govaert (1997)

Smaller values indicate a better trade-off between fit and complexity. The penalty per parameter is 2 for AIC, 3 for KIC, log((n + 2) / 24) for SABIC, log(n) for BIC and log(n) + 1 for CAIC; for samples beyond a few dozen units, AIC is therefore the most lenient and CAIC the most conservative, and heavier penalties favour fewer classes. ICL and AWE additionally penalize classification uncertainty, since overlapping classes increase EN; they consequently favour fewer and better-separated classes than BIC. CLC carries no per-parameter penalty, only the entropy term, and may favour many classes when these are well separated and few when they are not. CLC is defined here, as are ICL and AWE, on the entropy sum; some software reports a variant based on relative entropy, which is bounded by one and therefore imposes almost no penalty, and the two are not comparable.

Two conventions for the sample size

In a two-level model the sample size may be defined as the number of groups (here, 106 students) or the number of observations (here, 1,422 enrolments). latents reports every sample-size-dependent criterion under both conventions: columns ending in _groups use the number of groups and the posterior probabilities of the group classes for EN, and columns ending in _individual use the number of observations and the posterior probabilities of the profiles. Neither constitutes a uniquely correct multilevel BIC; each is a stated convention, and an analysis adopts one and applies it to every candidate. AIC and KIC do not depend on the sample size.

In a single-level model the two sample sizes coincide, and BIC, SABIC and CAIC are identical under both conventions. The entropy-based criteria are not: their _groups columns use the classification of the group classes, of which a single-level model has only one, so they carry no classification penalty and ICL reduces to BIC. For single-level models, the _individual columns of ICL, AWE and CLC should therefore be used.

The table of every candidate

as.data.frame() returns one row per candidate, containing every criterion under both conventions together with the log likelihood, the number of parameters, summaries of classification quality and diagnostics of estimation.

The minimum of each criterion

get_results(x, "best") reduces this table to one row per criterion and convention, giving the candidate at which the criterion attains its minimum, its numbers of classes and the minimum value. It identifies the candidate favoured by each criterion and makes no further inference.

get_results(models, "best")
#>    criterion  convention         candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model value
#> 1        aic        <NA> profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16703
#> 2        kic        <NA> profiles4_groups4          4               4   VVI 16769
#> 3        bic      groups profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16852
#> 4        bic individuals profiles3_groups3          3               3   VVI 16973
#> 5      sabic      groups profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16661
#> 6      sabic individuals profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16823
#> 7       caic      groups profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16903
#> 8       caic individuals profiles3_groups3          3               3   VVI 17011
#> 9        awe      groups profiles3_groups2          3               2   VVI 17169
#> 10       awe individuals profiles2_groups3          2               3   VVI 17398
#> 11       icl      groups profiles4_groups2          4               2   VVI 16881
#> 12       icl individuals profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 17140
#> 13       clc      groups profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16580
#> 14       clc individuals profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 16944

In this example the criteria favour 8 different candidates: BIC with students as units favours profiles4_groups3, BIC with enrolments as units profiles3_groups3, ICL with students as units profiles4_groups2, and AIC profiles6_groups4. Such disagreement is typical rather than anomalous. The criteria were derived for different purposes, and their penalties largely account for the pattern: AIC, with the lightest penalty, favours the largest candidate, whereas the entropy-based criteria favour smaller ones.

A minimum at the boundary of the grid, that is, at the largest number of profiles or group classes estimated, indicates that the criterion was still decreasing and that the range examined was too narrow. The range is then extended until the minimum lies in its interior. Where the criterion continues to decrease at every size the data can support, as is common in large samples, the magnitude of successive decreases becomes the relevant evidence (see below).

Plotting the criteria

plot() displays the criteria against the number of profiles, with one line per number of group classes and the minimum of each criterion marked. what selects criteria by column name, and what = "all" displays all of them.

plot(models)

plot(models, what = "bic_groups")

Where added classes stop paying off

Deltas

When a criterion decreases across the entire range, its minimum is uninformative, but the magnitude of each decrease is not. get_results(x, "deltas") reports, for every candidate, the decrease in a criterion relative to the neighbouring candidate with one profile fewer (delta_profile, from from_profile) and with one group class fewer (delta_group_class, from from_group_class). A positive value indicates that the additional class reduced the criterion, and a negative value that it increased it; candidates without such a neighbour in the grid have NA. BIC with groups as units is used unless using specifies another criterion.

get_results(models, "deltas")

With three group classes, the third profile reduces BIC by 85 and the fourth by 22, whereas the fifth increases it by 27 (shown as a negative decrease). The candidate with two profiles has no profile-wise delta because its neighbour, with one profile and three group classes, is not identified. Diminishing decreases indicate the point beyond which additional profiles capture detail rather than structure, and the first negative value marks where they cease to improve the criterion. The deltas are displayed for both directions: along the number of profiles (left) and along the number of group classes (right).

plot(models, what = "deltas")

The same display is available for any criterion:

plot(models, what = "deltas", using = "icl_individual")

Knees

The knee, or elbow, of a decreasing curve is the point at which it changes from steep to flat. get_results(x, "knees") locates it with a simplified, geometric version of the Kneedle algorithm (Satopää, Albrecht, Irwin and Raghavan, 2011):

  1. both axes, the number of classes and the criterion, are rescaled to the unit interval;
  2. a chord is drawn from the first candidate to the last;
  3. the knee is the candidate with the greatest perpendicular distance below the chord, and distance is that distance in rescaled units.

The smoothing and sensitivity thresholds of the original algorithm are omitted, so a nearly linear curve may still yield a knee with a very small distance; the distance therefore quantifies the strength of the bend as well as its location. A curve whose final value is not below its initial value has no knee, since a bend in an increasing criterion does not indicate diminishing returns.

Knees are computed along three families of curves: over the number of profiles at each number of group classes (direction = "profiles"), over the number of group classes at each number of profiles ("group_classes"), and over all candidates ordered by number of parameters ("parameters"). The columns from and to identify the endpoints of each curve and n_points its length.

get_results(models, "knees")
#>        direction            line  criterion              from                to n_points
#> 1       profiles   1 group class bic_groups profiles1_groups1 profiles6_groups1        6
#> 2       profiles 2 group classes bic_groups profiles2_groups2 profiles6_groups2        5
#> 3       profiles 3 group classes bic_groups profiles2_groups3 profiles6_groups3        5
#> 4       profiles 4 group classes bic_groups profiles2_groups4 profiles6_groups4        5
#> 5  group_classes       1 profile bic_groups profiles1_groups1 profiles1_groups1        1
#> 6  group_classes      2 profiles bic_groups profiles2_groups1 profiles2_groups4        4
#> 7  group_classes      3 profiles bic_groups profiles3_groups1 profiles3_groups4        4
#> 8  group_classes      4 profiles bic_groups profiles4_groups1 profiles4_groups4        4
#> 9  group_classes      5 profiles bic_groups profiles5_groups1 profiles5_groups4        4
#> 10 group_classes      6 profiles bic_groups profiles6_groups1 profiles6_groups4        4
#> 11    parameters  all candidates bic_groups profiles1_groups1 profiles6_groups4       21
#>       knee_candidate distance knee_without_largest stable                               note
#> 1  profiles2_groups1    0.544    profiles2_groups1   TRUE                                   
#> 2  profiles4_groups2    0.648    profiles3_groups2  FALSE moves when the largest is left out
#> 3  profiles4_groups3    0.750    profiles3_groups3  FALSE moves when the largest is left out
#> 4  profiles4_groups4    0.792    profiles3_groups4  FALSE moves when the largest is left out
#> 5               <NA>       NA                 <NA>     NA        fewer than three candidates
#> 6  profiles2_groups2    0.413    profiles2_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 7  profiles3_groups2    0.438    profiles3_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 8  profiles4_groups2    0.439    profiles4_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 9  profiles5_groups2    0.456    profiles5_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 10 profiles6_groups2    0.463    profiles6_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 11 profiles2_groups2    0.561    profiles2_groups2   TRUE

Because the chord terminates at the largest candidate estimated, the location of the knee depends on the extent of the grid: adding a candidate moves the chord and may move the knee. This dependence is assessed directly. knee_without_largest is the knee of the same curve with its final candidate removed, and stable is TRUE when the two coincide; a knee that shifts when the range is shortened by one candidate constitutes weak evidence. note explains every row for which no complete result is available:

note Meaning
empty a knee was found and is stable
fewer than three candidates a line needs three points for a knee
three candidates: stability not assessed stable needs four points
the criterion does not fall along this line no diminishing return to find
the curve does not bend below the line the curve is straight or bends upward
no knee when the largest is left out the shortened line has no knee
moves when the largest is left out the knee depends on the range fitted

With three group classes, the knee along the number of profiles is profiles4_groups3, at a distance of 0.75. Without the largest candidate it is profiles3_groups3, so stable is FALSE: the bend lies between three and four profiles, and which of the two is identified depends on the extent of the grid. The deltas locate the same region with less ambiguity, which is why the two are interpreted jointly.

The criterion over the whole grid

The heatmap displays all candidates simultaneously, shaded by the difference between each candidate’s criterion and the minimum in the grid. It uses the same criterion as the deltas and accepts the same using argument.

plot(models, what = "heatmap")

Are the classes distinct?

A candidate may fit the data well yet separate its classes poorly, leaving many units with uncertain class membership. Three statistics derived from the posterior probabilities of membership quantify separation.

  • Relative entropy, 1 - EN / (n log K) for K classes, ranges from 0, when every unit is equally likely to belong to every class, to 1, when every unit is classified with certainty. It summarizes an entire level in a single value and is undefined (NA) for a level with one class.
  • Average posterior probability (AvePP) of a class is the mean posterior probability of that class among the units modally assigned to it. Values of 0.7 to 0.8 or above are conventionally taken to indicate adequate separation (Nagin, 2005). Being class-specific, it reveals a single poorly separated class that entropy would average away.
  • Odds of correct classification (OCC) of a class is (p / (1 - p)) / (r / (1 - r)), where p is its AvePP and r its estimated proportion. It compares model-based classification with assignment by class proportion alone: values near 1 indicate no improvement, and values of 5 or more are conventionally taken to indicate adequate separation (Nagin, 2005).

The table of candidates summarizes each level by its relative entropy and the minimum, maximum and mean AvePP, and counts the classes below a cutoff (0.8 by default, set with cutoff). get_results(x, "classification") reports, for every class of every candidate, its size by modal assignment and by estimate, its AvePP, its OCC and the relative entropy of its level.

get_results(models, "classification")

plot(x, what = "diagnostics") displays relative entropy and the minimum AvePP across candidates, with the cutoff indicated; what = "entropy" and what = "avepp" display either one. For a single fitted candidate, plot_diagnostics() displays the posterior probability of each unit’s assigned class, each unit’s relative entropy, the class sizes and the matrix of average posterior probabilities, for the profiles and, when there are two or more group classes, for the group classes (what = "group_posteriors", etc.).

plot(models, what = "diagnostics")

Entropy and AvePP may diverge, and the divergence is informative. AvePP depends only on the posterior probability of each unit’s assigned class, whereas entropy depends on the full vector of posterior probabilities. A unit with posterior probabilities of 0.70, 0.10, 0.10 and 0.10 and a unit with 0.70 and 0.30 contribute equally to AvePP, but the former, whose uncertainty is distributed across all classes, reduces entropy considerably more. Moreover, entropy is more sensitive to a minority of highly uncertain units than to a majority of nearly certain ones. A level comprising mostly well-classified units and a tail of uncertain ones therefore exhibits moderate AvePP together with low entropy.

The two levels of a two-level model are classified on the basis of different amounts of information. A group’s class is inferred from all of its observations jointly, whereas an observation’s profile is inferred from its own responses alone; group classes are consequently classified with considerably greater certainty. For a single candidate, plot_diagnostics() displays both levels:

plot_diagnostics(get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3"),
                 what = "group_posteriors")

When all candidates separate their profiles poorly, such that no number of classes yields adequate entropy or minimum AvePP, the indicators do not discriminate well among individual observations. The number of classes is then determined from the information criteria and substantive interpretation, and the limited separation is reported as a limitation. In this situation modal class assignments are an unreliable substitute for the latent classes in subsequent analyses, and bias-corrected three-step estimators (r3step(), three_step()) should be used instead.

Classification quality is not in itself a criterion for the number of classes: models with fewer classes are generally better separated, so selection on entropy alone favours too few classes. It serves to discriminate between candidates that the information criteria do not distinguish, and it determines how the selected classes may be used, for example whether modal assignments can represent them in subsequent analyses.

Can the estimate be trusted?

Estimation checks

Because the likelihood is multimodal, a solution replicated from several random starts is more credible than one obtained from a single start. An estimate on the boundary of the parameter space, such as a variance at its lower bound or a class with negligible membership, indicates a model too complex for the data. plot(x, what = "trust") represents each candidate by a tile labelled with the number of starts that reached its maximum likelihood and shaded by the first problem detected:

Status Meaning
best replicated converged within the interior of the parameter space, with the maximum likelihood reached by more than one start
best found once as above, but the maximum likelihood was reached by a single start
on a boundary an estimate lies on the boundary of the parameter space
not converged the EM algorithm terminated before meeting its convergence criterion
not fitted (x) not identified, or estimation failed (the error is retained in the table) 
plot(models, what = "trust")

A candidate whose maximum was found only once should be re-estimated with more starts before it is selected, together with the remainder of the grid (see Random starts). If re-estimation increases its likelihood, the earlier solution was a local maximum and is superseded; entropy and AvePP often increase as well. A higher AvePP is never a ground for preferring one solution of a given candidate over another: the maximum likelihood solution is the estimate. The columns converged, boundary, n_best_replicated, warnings and error of the table of candidates report the same diagnostics. A candidate on a boundary whose smallest class holds about one observation is a degenerate solution rather than a class; re-estimating the grid with boundary = "exclude" replaces it with the best solution in the interior of the parameter space (see Random starts).

The smallest class

A class comprising a very small proportion of units is difficult to interpret and is estimated from little data. plot(x, what = "smallest") displays the estimated proportion of the smallest class of every candidate, with a reference line at 5%, a conventional threshold rather than a rule.

plot(models, what = "smallest")

All of the plots together

plot(x, what = "selection") returns the deltas, the heatmap, the smallest class, the estimation diagnostics and the classification diagnostics as a list of plots displayed in sequence. using sets the criterion for the first two and cutoff the AvePP threshold for the last.

plot(models, what = "selection")

How the profiles divide

The clustering tree shows how the profiles of each model are partitioned in the model with one additional profile: each profile is linked to the profiles of the larger model that receive its observations (Zappia and Oshlack, 2018). A profile that divides cleanly into two suggests a substantive distinction, whereas a profile formed from several profiles of the smaller model suggests a reallocation of observations rather than a refinement.

plot(models, what = "tree")

Comparing chosen candidates

Once the evidence has reduced the choice to a few candidates, compare_models() tabulates them side by side, specified by label or by numbers of classes. The table adds each candidate’s difference in BIC from the smallest value among those compared (delta_bic) and its BIC weight, exp(-delta_bic / 2) normalized over the compared candidates, which approximates the posterior probability of each model under equal prior probabilities, assuming one of them is correct (Wagenmakers and Farrell, 2004). The weights are conditional on the set of candidates compared.

comparison <- compare_models(models, "profiles3_groups3", "profiles4_groups3",
                             "profiles4_groups2")
comparison
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model              Profiles  Group classes   k    LogLik       BIC   ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8  Group entropy  Group min AvePP
#> -----------------  --------  -------------  --  --------  --------  -----  ------  --------  -------  ---------  -----  -------------  ---------------
#> profiles3_groups3         3              3  38  -8348.43  16874.07  21.92   0.000  17622.03     0.79       0.85      0           0.80             0.86
#> profiles4_groups3         4              3  51  -8307.15  16852.14   0.00   1.000  18014.13     0.74       0.80      0           0.82             0.87
#> profiles4_groups2         4              2  47  -8326.19  16871.57  19.43   0.000  18021.23     0.74       0.79      1           0.94             0.98
plot(comparison)

The fitted model corresponding to a row is extracted with get_candidate(), by label or by numbers of classes.

chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
chosen
#> Two-level latent profile analysis: 4 profiles, 3 group classes
#> 1422 individuals in 106 groups; varying diagonal residual covariance (VVI)
#> Log likelihood: -8307.154320 | AIC: 16716.309 | BIC (groups): 16852.144
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 48 | best start: 3/3
#> 
#>  profile browse lectures forum_read forum_post attendance count proportion
#>        1  0.412    0.232      0.490      0.383      0.309   497      0.350
#>        2 -0.564   -0.561     -0.695     -0.676     -0.656   392      0.276
#>        3 -1.113   -0.685     -1.200     -0.880     -1.417   202      0.142
#>        4  0.728    0.734      0.821      0.763      1.180   331      0.233
#> 
#> Variances and standard errors: get_results(x, "profiles"). 
#> Every other table: get_results(x, what = ), or get_results(x, "all").

Testing one more class

The conventional likelihood ratio test is invalid for comparing mixtures with k and k + 1 classes, because the null model lies on the boundary of the parameter space of the alternative, where the test statistic does not follow its usual asymptotic distribution. bootstrap_lrt() approximates the null distribution by parametric bootstrap (McLachlan, 1987; Nylund, Asparouhov and Muthén, 2007): data sets are simulated from the fitted null model, both models are re-estimated on each, and the observed statistic is referred to the simulated distribution. With B simulated data sets of which b yield a statistic at least as large as the observed one, the p-value is (b + 1) / (B + 1), which is bounded below by 1 / (B + 1). If any replicate fails an estimation check, the p-value is withheld rather than computed from the remaining replicates. The example uses 19 replicates, for which the smallest attainable p-value is 0.05; applied analyses should use 99 or more.

smaller <- get_candidate(models, "profiles3_groups3")
larger <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
test <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = course_engagement,
                      iter = 19, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
test
#> Parametric bootstrap likelihood-ratio comparison
#> Null: 3 profiles, 3 group classes; alternative: 4 profiles, 3 group classes
#> Observed statistic: 82.548767
#> p-value: 0.05 (Monte Carlo SE 0.0487) from 19 of 19 valid replicates
plot(test)

Putting the evidence together

No algorithm converts this evidence into a number of classes, and latents applies none. A defensible decision is reached by examining the evidence in a fixed sequence and reporting each step:

  1. Analytic decisions: report the number of random starts, whether starts at a variance bound were excluded (boundary), any centring or scaling, the treatment of missing values, and the number of observations with no observed indicator.
  2. Sample-size convention: specify the convention before examining any criterion and apply it consistently.
  3. Criterion minima: examine the minima under that convention, noting where the criteria agree and the direction in which they disagree. A minimum at the boundary of the grid requires an extended grid.
  4. Deltas and knees: where the criteria decrease throughout, examine the magnitude of successive decreases and report the knee with its distance and stability.
  5. Classification quality: for the remaining candidates, report relative entropy and the minimum AvePP and OCC at each level.
  6. Estimation diagnostics: verify replication of the maximum likelihood, the absence of boundary estimates and the size of the smallest class; re-estimate candidates whose maximum was found only once.
  7. Likelihood ratio test: when the evidence is equivocal, test the leading candidate against its neighbour with the bootstrap likelihood ratio test.
  8. Substantive interpretation: among candidates that the statistics do not distinguish, select the one whose classes are distinct and substantively meaningful for the research question, and state the rationale.

The tables underlying each step are returned by the functions above, so that the reported decision can be reproduced from the reported evidence.

Functions

Call Result
enumerate_classes(…, n_starts = , centering = , scaling = , missing = “fiml”) The same starts, centring, scaling and missing-data handling for every candidate
enumerate_classes(…, boundary = “exclude”) Starts with a variance at its lower bound set aside for every candidate
as.data.frame(models) One row per candidate: every criterion, classification summaries and checks
get_results(models, “best”) The candidate at the minimum of each criterion and convention
plot(models), plot(models, what = “bic_groups”), what = “all” Criteria across the candidates, lowest ringed
get_results(models, “deltas”, using = ) Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer
plot(models, what = “deltas”, using = ) The decreases along profiles and along group classes
get_results(models, “knees”, using = ) Chord-distance knee of each line, with its stability
plot(models, what = “heatmap”, using = ) Distance of every candidate from the lowest criterion
get_results(models, “classification”) Size, AvePP, OCC and entropy of every class of every candidate
get_results(models, “candidates”, cutoff = ) The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff
plot(models, what = “diagnostics”, “entropy” or “avepp”, cutoff = ) Relative entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates
get_results(fit, “entropy”) Relative entropy of one fit at each level, over the classified units
plot_diagnostics(fit), what = “group_posteriors” and the like Certainty, uncertainty, sizes and AvePP of one fit, profiles and group classes
plot(models, what = “trust”) Convergence, boundary and replication of every candidate
plot(models, what = “smallest”) Share of the smallest class of every candidate
plot(models, what = “selection”) Deltas, heatmap, smallest class, trust and diagnostics together
plot(models, what = “tree”) How the profiles divide as more are added
compare_models(models, “name”, …) Chosen candidates side by side, with BIC weights
get_candidate(models, “name”) One fitted candidate
bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data, iter) Bootstrap likelihood ratio test of k against k + 1 classes
